accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 2 and the Years 3–4 spelling appendix (word families based on common words: solve, solution, solver, dissolve, insoluble), Common Core L.3.4c, and etymologies in the Online Etymology Dictionary and Merriam-Webster: act, actor, action, react and active from Latin agere/actus; fact from facere; tractor from trahere (to pull); cactus from Greek kaktos; kindle from Old Norse kynda, unrelated to kind; solar from sol; helmet from helm; helium from Greek helios. Unbreakable, helpless, disagreement and rebuilding were peeled by hand.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips: shared letters treated as shared family (step 2 prediction on cactus, fact/tractor cards, kindle and helmet in the challenge, p2, m6), any affix on any root (unact and actful rejected in step 1, m5), a spelling change read as a different family (step 3 prediction on solution, m3), a prefix or suffix mistaken for the root (step 4 prediction on disagreement, the un/ness options for unhappiness), and confusing word jobs (invention or inventive for a person who invents).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwfam builds words by dragging prefix and suffix tiles onto the root act with decoys that make non-words, sorts look-alike words out of the family, matches solve-family words to clues where the root is spelled solu-, peels words into prefix, root and suffix chunks, and files a create/invent family into four word jobs. No other lab combines building on a root with meaning checks; flagunpre (un- only), flagsfxrule (spelling changes) and flagdecode (reading odd words) do not, and lab_distinct stayed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the idea from feedback: dropping -ful on act returns 'Actful is not a word. Not every ending fits every root'; filing fact in the family returns 'Fact has a, c and t, but it means something true, not doing'; choosing solver for the answer-to-a-problem clue prompts '-er names a person. Is the clue about a person?'; tapping un in unbreakable returns 'un- is a prefix. It sits at the front and changes the meaning'; misfiling creator says '-or names who does it'.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: actor, action and react only share letters (step 1 shows each still means doing), cactus is in the family because it has a-c-t (the sort rejects it with its meaning), solution is not family because the spelling changed (the clue match confirms solu- is the same root), and dis or ment as the root of disagreement (the peel step rejects both).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six questions with tagged wrong options and specific messages: a family word chosen as the odd one out ('helpful is in the family: help + ful, full of help'), a look-alike chosen as family (fact, cactus, solar, sold), a prefix or suffix chosen as the root (un, ness, including the y to i change), and the wrong word job for a person (invention: -ion makes a thing; inventive: -ive describes).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid (≤ 6.5) and adult (≤ 9.5) limits. Kid paragraphs use one idea per short sentence, introduce root, prefix and suffix with one example each (help, unhelpful, helper), and repeat the meaning test with helmet. The lab names parts the same way the curriculum does: root word, prefix, suffix.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step teaches one move (build, test meaning, follow a spelling shift, peel, file by job) and every item explanation states why the right answer fits and why the others do not, for example 'A solver is a person and a solution is an answer'.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, 1.5x) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: six affix tiles sit in two rows below the root, the two sort boxes and four job boxes fit in a 2 by 2 grid above the feedback box, and clue words fit in a 2 by 2 grid. The affix row, sort boxes and job boxes were moved up after the first screenshots showed them overlapping the wrapped feedback box, and the job feedback was rewritten as a full sentence.

accessibility.evidence: Everything on the canvas has a button: each affix (Add suffix or), both sort choices, the four solve words, each chunk of the word to peel (Choose break), and the four word jobs. The canvas aria-label describes the current card or word after every move, challenge feedback is an aria-live status, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
